chunk_findings.detail: `landed_leftovers_only` skips the file-content check for every merge commit: when `len(parents) > 1`, it only verifies that each parent after the first is an ancestor of `base`, then `continue`s. A merge commit’s own merge resolution can add arbitrary non-pin files while satisfying that check. Example: `base`/main is at B and `item.merged_sha` is B; create merge commit M with `git merge --no-ff --no-commit B`, edit `src/foo.py`, and commit. Both parents of M are ancestors of `base`, so `base..HEAD` contains only M. The function sees M, finds the second parent is on `base`, `continue`s, returns `True`, and `_classify` marks the tree `action = "remove"`. Cleanup then deletes the worktree, losing `src/foo.py`, which exists nowhere on `base`. The merge commit itself must be diffed (`diff-tree -m` or equivalent) and required to contain only pinned files, otherwise a merge commit is unsafe to classify as “merge-main/pin commits only”.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:landed_leftovers_only

chunk_findings.detail: When the re-proof fails because the worktree is “no longer only landed leftovers”, `_remove_planned` returns a `kept ...` report line but does not update `t.action`/`t.kind`/`t.done`. `apply` receives `plan` by reference, and the same function updates `t` in the `dispose_tree(...).outcome == "refused"` path explicitly so later consumers of `plan` see the final decision (the function docstring also says `t` is updated when kept). Input example: `plan.worktrees` contains an ahead tree with `t.action = "remove"`; between survey and apply the worktree gains a non-leftover commit, so `landed_leftovers_only` returns false. The returned report says the tree was kept, but `t.action` remains `"remove"`, so the plan still reports it as selected for removal.

chunk_findings.detail: `landed_leftovers_only` treats a root commit as safe to delete even when it contains arbitrary non-pin files. For a commit with no parents, `git diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r <sha>` is run without `--root`; for a root commit this succeeds and emits no file names, so `set(files.out.split()) <= set(pins)` is vacuously true. Concretely, a clean worktree associated with a landed item whose checked-out branch was replaced with an orphan branch of the same name and which has one root commit adding `src/foo.py` will return `True`, leading `_classify` to set `kind="merged"` and `action="remove"`, and cleanup will remove the branch, losing the only copy of `src/foo.py`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:landed_leftovers_only (line 568)

chunk_findings.detail: After `dispose_tree` returns, the new forced branch deletion `W.git(root, "branch", "-D", t.branch)` is not wrapped in `unless_claimed()`, unlike the branch deletion in `apply`’s `plan.stale_branches` loop a few lines below. Concretely, when `dispose_tree` removed the worktree but left the branch (`d.removed=True, d.branch_left=True`), the branch is now a free branch and another ddflow process can claim/check it out before this unguarded `git branch -D` runs; the command force-deletes that now-live branch. The later `stale_branches` path exists to avoid exactly this claimed-branch deletion race, and this new path bypasses it.

chunk_findings.detail: `elif t.ahead and leftovers:` treats any truthy `t.ahead` as a positive commit count. The existing code at line 541 already uses `tw.ahead >= 0` to mean “count succeeded” and otherwise emits `cannot count commits ahead of {wt.base}`, so `_tree_state` can put the `-1` sentinel in `t.ahead` when commit counting fails. For a tree with that `-1` sentinel, no dirty files, and an already-landed item, `leftovers` can be true thanks to `landed_leftovers_only` succeeding on an empty/safe `git log base..HEAD`, causing the branch to say `-1 commit(s) left` and set `action = "remove"` even though this is the “cannot count commits ahead” escape hatch. The condition should be `t.ahead > 0 and leftovers`; `-1` is not a count of leftovers.

chunk_findings.detail: The landed-leftovers proof is not atomic with the forced worktree removal. Given branch tip `C1`, `landed_leftovers_only` can return true; if another process commits `C2` to that branch before `dispose_tree(..., forced_by=proof)` runs, `dispose_tree` may still remove the worktree even though it is no longer only landed leftovers. The later `update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> C1` happens only after the worktree is already gone and only protects the branch ref, not the removed worktree. Cleanup therefore deletes a worktree that was active and no longer satisfied the proof.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:_remove_planned

chunk_findings.detail: `files.out.split()` splits `git diff-tree --name-only` output on arbitrary whitespace, but the command does not use `-z`, so Git paths containing spaces are not parsed as single path names. This can misclassify commits. Concretely, with `pins == ["a.pin", "b.pin"]`, one non-pin file literally named `a.pin b.pin` is emitted as a single line `a.pin b.pin`; `.split()` yields `{"a.pin", "b.pin"}`, which is a subset of `pins`, so `landed_leftovers_only` returns True and cleanup offers removal for a commit that touched no actual pin file. Use `-z` and split on NUL to make the comparison path-accurate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:landed_leftovers_only

chunk_findings.detail: When the `update-ref` branch deletion succeeds, the code replaces `d` with `Disposal("removed", had_branch=True)`, but it never sets `removed=True` or `why`. `dispose_tree` returns a `Disposal` whose `outcome` and `removed` are separate fields: the same function later checks `d.outcome == "refused"` and then uses `d.removed` for the kept/removed message. In this path `d.removed` is left at its default false and `d.why` is empty, so the final return evaluates `d.why.splitlines()[0][:120]` on an empty string and raises `IndexError`. Concretely, a landed leftover worktree whose branch is deleted after `dispose_tree` leaves it will be removed and then `apply` crashes.

chunk_findings.detail: The branch OID used for `update-ref -d` is captured *after* `landed_leftovers_only()` has already validated the worktree as only merge/pin leftovers, but the proof is never bound to the OID that was validated. If the branch receives a new commit between that check and the later `rev-parse` (a clean commit into the yet-unremoved worktree), then `tip` is that new commit. `dispose_tree()` removes the worktree and the following `update-ref -d refs/heads/{t.branch} tip` deletes the new commit, which may be real work. The OID should be captured at the same moment it is proved to be leftovers; using a later `rev-parse` means `update-ref` no longer “only if it is still at the proved tip”.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous race still holds. The triage's probe only narrows the window, it does not make the landed-leftovers proof atomic with the forced worktree removal. The in-scope defect was that the worktree is removed, not that the branch ref is updated. Even with a clean re-check immediately before disposal, another process can commit `C2` to the same branch after that re-check and before `dispose_tree(..., forced_by=proof)`; the worktree is still force-removed even though the branch is no longer only landed leftovers. The later `update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> C1` runs after the worktree is gone, so it may leave the branch ref at `C2` while the worktree and any untracked files in it are lost.

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 2 still holds. The proof string produced by `landed_leftovers_only(...)` is not bound to the OID it inspected. In the interleaving: branch `B` is at leftover tip `C1`, the proof passes, and then another process commits `C2` in that worktree before the next line reads `refs/heads/{t.branch}` into `tip`. Now `tip` is `C2`, not the proved `C1`. `dispose_tree(..., forced_by=proof)` forcibly removes the worktree while it is no longer only landed leftovers, and the subsequent `update-ref -d refs/heads/B tip` deletes `C2`, even though `C2` was never proved to be a leftover. If `C2` lands after the `rev-parse` but before `dispose_tree`, the branch survives but the now-non-leftover worktree is still force-removed. The old-value guard only proves `tip` did not change after it was read; it does not prove that `tip` is the tip validated by `landed_leftovers_only`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:_remove_planned

chunk_findings.detail: The TOCTOU race remains. After the new clean re-check proves the branch tip `C1` is only landed leftovers but before the forced removal, another process can commit `C2` in that worktree. Then `dispose_tree(..., forced_by=proof)` runs `git worktree remove --force` and deletes the worktree even though it is no longer only landed leftovers. The later `git update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> C1` fails because the ref is now `C2`; the surviving branch ref does not preserve the removed worktree the other process was using. The new test `tests/test_cleanup_landed_leftovers.py:test_apply_removes_tree_and_branch_of_a_landed_item` only exercises single-process removal, so it does not answer this interleaving.

chunk_findings.detail: The prior three TOCTOU findings still hold. The added `moved`/`work.dirty` re-check at `W.git(Path(t.path), "rev-parse", "--verify", "HEAD")` happens before `dispose_tree(..., forced_by=proof)`, but nothing serializes the interval up to `git worktree remove --force`. chunk_findings.detail: The residual TOCTOU from previous findings 1 and 3 still holds. After `_remove_planned` performs its final HEAD/dirty re-check that proves the branch tip is the landed-leftover commit, but before `dispose_tree(..., forced_by=proof)` runs `git worktree remove --force`, another process can write a new untracked file or commit to the same branch in that worktree. `git worktree remove --force` then deletes the worktree anyway, and the later compare-and-delete `git update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> C1` cannot restore the removed worktree. chunk_findings.detail: The prior TOCTOU findings are not fully answered. After `moved` is computed false because `HEAD == tip`, another process can commit `C2` in the same worktree. `dispose_tree(..., allow_ahead=bool(proof))` still removes the worktree: an unforced `git worktree remove` does not refuse a clean worktree merely because its branch advanced, so the worktree is deleted even though it is no longer only landed leftovers. The later compare-and-delete `git update-ref -d refs/heads/<branch> tip` then fails and preserves `C2`, but the worktree is already gone, which is the bug this change is meant to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: In the `if work.dirty or not work.readable or moved:` branch, `_remove_planned` returns a `kept {t.name}: the tree changed since it was proved to be leftovers` line but does not update `t.action`, `t.kind`, or `t.done`. The same function clears these in the `not tip` branch and the `d.outcome == "refused"` branch, and the pre-change `apply` code cleared them whenever a tree was kept. Concrete input: a plan tree has `t.action == "remove"`; a file is modified after the survey; `_remove_planned` returns the kept message but leaves `t.action` as `"remove"`, so a report serialized from `plan.trees` can show this kept tree as remove.

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not exercise the interleaving its name and the triage claim describe. `(tree / "scratch.txt").write_text("written after the check\n")` runs before `W.remove` is called, so any initial dirty check or proof precondition in `W.remove` sees the pre-existing untracked file and returns `not ok`.
